messages.subject: computing Hessians with auto-dif
parts:
If anyone is interested in auto-dif for literally
computing Hessians, the way to go is to write a templated
forward-mode auto dif. (I still haven't gotten my head
around how a Hessian-vector product can be done more
easily.)

This is MUCH MUCH easier than reverse-mode auto-dif
in that it doesn't require any malloc.

Reverse-mode propagates the chain rule back from
the dependent variable to all of its subexpressions,
including the independent variables we care about.

Forward-mode propagates derivatives forward from a
single independent variable to all of the expressions
that depend on it.

The basic type is:

struct fvar {
fvar(double val) : _val(val), _adj(1.0) { }
fvar(double val, double adj) : _val(val), _adj(adj) { }
double _val;
double _adj;
}

And then operators just push the auto-dif through one
step of the chain rule w.r.t. the operation:

// d/dx (x + b) = 1
fvar operator+(fvar& a, double bv) {
return fvar(a._val + bv,
a._adj * 1);
}

// d/dx (x * b) = b
fvar operator*(fvar& a, double bv) {
return fvar(a._val * bv,
a._adj * bv);
}

// d/dx sqrt(x) = 1/(2 * sqrt(x))
fvar sqrt(fvar& a) {
return fvar(sqrt(a._val),
a._adj * (1 / (2 * sqrt(a._val))));


and so on.

The next step is to template out the double, so you have:

template <typename T>
struct fvar {
fvar(T val) : _val(val), _adj(1.0) { }
fvar(T val, T adj) : _val(val), _adj(adj) { }
T _val;
T _adj;
}

You might want a reference there for (const T& val).

The templated form of operators looks like:

template <typename T>
fvar operator*(fvar<T>& a, double bv) {
return fvar<T>(a._val * bv,
a._adj * bv);
}

A suitable T will define constructors and assignments
for doubles (making T(1) valid) and also for arithmetic.

For example, stan::agrad::var is such a T.

You then compute the Hessian of f:R^N -> R^N
a column at a time by moving through the arguments,
and for each one, using a forward-mode auto-dif
variable templated on stan::agrad::var. Take
the result, grab its adj_ value, and then calculate
its gradient by a call to reverse mode auto dif.

The forward-mode part of this is cheap enough that
the cost shouldn't be noticeably more than running
K reverse-mode auto difs.

- Bob
